query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount (~1-2 at.%) of a ductility-enhancing element such as Zr into the equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance without compromising its high‐temperature mechanical properties and BCC structural stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW known for excellent high-temperature performance (~1600 °C) but poor room-temperature ductility and unverified experimental irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Add a minor fraction (approximately 1-2 at.%) of Zr to the base NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing for ductility; high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical performance tests; irradiation experiments using helium and heavy ions (e.g., Kr and He) at fluences typical for assessing irradiation-induced defect formation and blistering.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion and slight compositional modification that promotes dislocation mobility and self-healing mechanisms, while preserving the long-range BCC order.
generation.mechanism: The minor addition of Zr is expected to enhance dislocation mobility by reducing stress concentrations and promoting defect recombination, which improves ductility and mitigates irradiation-induced defect accumulation (e.g., He bubble or blister formation); meanwhile, the overall BCC structure remains stable, ensuring minimal impact on high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the Zr-alloyed variant will exhibit increased elongation at room temperature, show reduced signs of irradiation-induced damage (like smaller or fewer helium bubbles and blisters), and maintain comparable high-temperature strength and phase stability.
generation.baseline: NbMoTaW alloy without Zr, characterized by high strength at elevated temperatures but limited ductility at room temperature and uncertain irradiation performance.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated under standard room-temperature mechanical testing and under irradiation conditions representative of reactor-relevant dual-beam (Kr and He) exposure, with performance maintained up to 1600 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvements in ductility and irradiation tolerance are uncertain, and there is a risk that the added Zr could lead to unforeseen phase segregation or precipitation under prolonged high-temperature exposure or extreme irradiation conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of standard NbMoTaW alloy and one set alloyed with 1-2 at.% Zr. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility (e.g., % elongation to fracture), high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical tests to verify strength retention, and irradiation tests (using sequential Kr and He ion implantation) to evaluate irradiation-induced defect formation and blistering.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Microstructural characterization post-irradiation (defect density, He bubble/blister size and distribution via TEM or SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-alloyed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and/or irradiation tolerance (i.e., reduction in defect size/density or blister formation), or if they exhibit compromised high-temperature mechanical performance or BCC phase instability compared to the baseline NbMoTaW, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The HEAs are also resistant to forming large defect clusters compared with binary nickel alloy systems and have the self-healing effect. Dislocation loops and lines can significantly affect the hardening and embrittlement, but in CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi, the density of dislocation loops after irradiation by Ni ions was higher than that of binary and ternary nickel alloys, and most of these loops had a smaller size []. The reasons for the self-healing of HEAs include high atomic stress and lattice distortion caused by the large difference in atomic size, which lead to the amorphization followed by crystallization of the alloy [,], and the similarity of vacancy and interstitial migration energies, which improve the defect annihilation []. Thus, the structural features of the HEAs affect the radiation resistance.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Composition and Structure of Initial CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi HEAs
cited_evidence.text: The elemental content and main phases of CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were preserved despite successive irradiation with krypton (280 keV, 5 × 1015 cm−2) and helium (40 keV, 2 × 1017 cm−2) ions; new phases did not emerge, but several blisters formed on the surface of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, although with a smaller average size than in Ni. Fewer large blisters formed in the HEA probably because of lattice distortion, low defect mobility and weakened helium bubble formation [,]. It can be seen that Kr irradiation enhances the surface damage leading to blister formation at room temperature compared to He-only irradiation, which was carried out in []. Analysis of the results of the study of macrostresses and density of dislocations in HEAs showed that the main changes obtained as a result of sample irradiation are probably associated with the formation, interaction and migration of radiation-induced defects and their clusters, which modified stresses in the alloys. reading.lever: Add a small amount of a ductility-enhancing element (e.g., Zr) to the NbMoTaW base alloy.
reading.why: Introducing a minor ductile element, as seen in related BCC MEAs with good room-temperature elongation, is expected to enhance dislocation mobility and self-healing without compromising high‐temperature BCC stability or irradiation tolerance.
